title: 8 · Pitfalls
section: 1 · A library that cannot express the target
text:
1 · A library that cannot express the target
So far the response was biomass, which grows roughly as a smooth function of the season. Now try the same pipeline on leaf area index (LAI), which rises, peaks, and then falls as leaves senesce. We only change var = "lai".

trl <- make_trajectories(traj, drv, var = "lai")
gl  <- gram_stats(Theta, trl)
cvl <- cv_blocked(Theta, trl, gl, fit_ols)                 # cubic polynomial library, all 13 terms
round(evaluate(cvl$pred, trl), 3)

trajectory_rmse  fixed_day_rmse   maturity_rmse 
          0.885           1.212           0.972 


Compare with the lookup (the genotype’s mean curve in other years), and with a different library: a B-spline basis in thermal time, which is flexible in the season clock, plus the other drivers linearly.

lookup_all <- function(tr_) {
  base <- array(NA_real_, dim(tr_$Y))
  for (y in seq_along(tr_$years)) base[, y, ] <- apply(tr_$Y[, -y, , drop = FALSE], c(1, 3), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
  for (g in 1:dim(base)[1]) for (y in 1:dim(base)[2]) {
    v <- base[g, y, ]; ok <- which(!is.nan(v)); v[is.nan(v)] <- v[max(ok)]; base[g, y, ] <- v; base[g, y, 1] <- tr_$Y[g, y, 1] }
  base
}
df <- 6; TT <- drv$U[, , 1]; B <- bs(as.vector(TT), df = df)
Th_spl <- array(NA_real_, c(dim(TT), 1 + df + 3), dimnames = list(NULL, NULL, c("1", paste0("B", 1:df), "DL", "RAW", "RAD")))
Th_spl[, , 1] <- 1
for (j in 1:df) Th_spl[, , 1 + j] <- B[, j]
for (j in 1:3)  Th_spl[, , 1 + df + j] <- drv$U[, , j + 1]
cvs <- cv_blocked(Th_spl, trl, gram_stats(Th_spl, trl), fit_ols)

res <- rbind(`cubic polynomial` = evaluate(cvl$pred, trl), `B-spline in TT` = evaluate(cvs$pred, trl), `no-weather lookup` = evaluate(lookup_all(trl), trl))
round(res, 3)

                  trajectory_rmse fixed_day_rmse maturity_rmse
cubic polynomial            0.885          1.212         0.972
B-spline in TT              0.526          0.664         0.539
no-weather lookup           0.473          0.687         0.637


The summary table hides when each model is wrong. The error of every held-out trajectory, by day:

lk <- lookup_all(trl)
err_by_day <- function(P) sapply(2:dim(P)[3], function(d) { ok <- !is.na(trl$Y[, , d]); sqrt(mean((P[, , d][ok] - trl$Y[, , d][ok])^2)) })
nd <- dim(trl$Y)[3] - 1
d <- data.frame(das = rep(2:(nd + 1) + trl$das0 - 1, 3), rmse = c(err_by_day(cvl$pred), err_by_day(cvs$pred), err_by_day(lk)),
                model = factor(rep(c("cubic polynomial", "B-spline in TT", "no-weather lookup"), each = nd), c("cubic polynomial", "B-spline in TT", "no-weather lookup")))
d <- d[d$das <= 15 + 140, ]
ggplot(d, aes(das, rmse, colour = model)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(dgxe[c("red", "green", "blue")])) + labs(x = "days after sowing", y = "held-out LAI RMSE", colour = NULL) + theme_dgxe()














ImportantPitfall



The spline library is far better than the polynomial for LAI (0.53 versus 0.89 trajectory RMSE) and beats the lookup at day 113 and at maturity, but over whole trajectories the lookup is still slightly ahead (0.47). The polynomial is clearly worse than the lookup everywhere. A polynomial in standardised drivers cannot make the rise-and-fall shape of LAI. When a model fails, look at the library before the fitting method: a better regression cannot find a term that is not in the dictionary.

title: 8 · Pitfalls
section: 2 · Collinear drivers: stable curves, unstable coefficients
text:
2 · Collinear drivers: stable curves, unstable coefficients
Thermal time and day length move together (correlation 0.97). Fit the same model separately on the odd and even years and compare.

odd <- which(tr$years %% 2 == 1); even <- which(tr$years %% 2 == 0)
fo <- fit_years(gram, odd, fit_ols); fe <- fit_years(gram, even, fit_ols)
tab <- round(cbind(odd_years = fo$mu, even_years = fe$mu), 3); rownames(tab) <- gram$names; tab[c("TT", "TT^2", "DL", "DL^2"), ]

     odd_years even_years
TT      -0.063     -0.037
TT^2    -0.036     -0.031
DL       0.045      0.020
DL^2    -0.055     -0.051


The coefficients for TT and DL are quite different between the halves. But what matters is the growth rate the model predicts:

Tbar <- apply(Theta, c(2, 3), mean)
r_odd <- as.vector(Tbar %*% fo$mu); r_even <- as.vector(Tbar %*% fe$mu)
c(correlation = cor(r_odd, r_even), max_difference_t_per_ha_day = max(abs(r_odd - r_even)))

                correlation max_difference_t_per_ha_day 
                0.998197498                 0.009107564 








NoteIdea



When drivers are collinear, the data constrain the combination, not each coefficient. The predicted rate is stable; individual coefficients are not. That is why step 6 reads curves, never single coefficients, and why a sparse model’s choice between TT and DL should not be over-interpreted.

title: 8 · Pitfalls
section: 3 · Small daily errors, large accumulated errors
text:
3 · Small daily errors, large accumulated errors
The regression is on daily increments. The prediction is a running total of those increments, so small biases add up.

cv <- cv_blocked(Theta, tr, gram, fit_ssr, k = 12)
inc_err <- numeric(0)
for (g in seq_along(tr$genotypes)) for (y in seq_along(tr$years)) { n <- tr$nend[g, y]
  inc_err <- c(inc_err, diff(cv$pred[g, y, 1:(n + 1)]) - diff(tr$Y[g, y, 1:(n + 1)])) }
c(daily_increment_rmse = sqrt(mean(inc_err^2)), rollout_rmse = unname(evaluate(cv$pred, tr)[1]))

daily_increment_rmse         rollout_rmse 
          0.02801567           0.52096960 


A tiny daily error can produce a large accumulated one, so always judge the model on the rollout, never on one-step fit.

title: 6 · Reading the model
text: You needa fitting method and the objects from step 5.You getthe final equation, and one curve per driver showing how it affects growth.

title: 6 · Reading the model
text:
The final model
For reading (not for validating) we fit once on all years. Validation told us the model generalises; now we look at what it learned.

f  <- fit_years(gram, seq_along(tr$years), fit_ssr, k = 12)
mu <- f$mu                                      # shared coefficients (all genotypes)
round(setNames(mu[f$support], f$names[f$support]), 4)

      1      TT    TT^2    TT^3      DL    DL^2    DL^3     RAW   RAW^2     RAD 
 0.1551 -0.0355 -0.0290  0.0116  0.0191 -0.0538  0.0184  0.0110 -0.0127  0.0073 
  RAD^2   RAD^3 
-0.0025 -0.0004 


This is the shared growth rule, written in standardised drivers (mean 0, standard deviation 1):
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}\,\text{biomass}}{\mathrm{d}t} = 0.155 \;-\; 0.036\,\text{TT} - 0.029\,\text{TT}^2 + 0.012\,\text{TT}^3 + 0.019\,\text{DL} - 0.054\,\text{DL}^2 + \dots
\]
The coefficients of a polynomial are hard to interpret one by one, so we plot what the equation does instead.

title: 6 · Reading the model
text:
Growth rate through the season
Apply the rule to the weather of each year. Each thin line is one year; the thick line is the average.

rate <- function(Z) as.vector(library_matrix(Z) %*% mu)                  # Z: n x 4 matrix of standardised drivers
ny <- length(tr$years); nd <- dim(Theta)[2]
R  <- sapply(seq_len(ny), function(y) as.vector(Theta[y, , ] %*% mu))       # day x year
d  <- data.frame(das = rep(seq_len(nd) + tr$das0 - 1, ny), year = rep(tr$years, each = nd), rate = as.vector(R))
d  <- d[d$das <= 15 + max(tr$nend) - 1, ]
ggplot(d, aes(das, rate, group = year)) + geom_line(colour = dgxe[["sky"]], linewidth = 0.4, alpha = 0.7) +
  stat_summary(aes(group = 1), fun = mean, geom = "line", colour = dgxe[["blue"]], linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = "days after sowing", y = "biomass growth rate (t/ha/day)") + theme_dgxe()

title: 6 · Reading the model
section: The effect of one driver: accumulated local effects
text:
The effect of one driver: accumulated local effects
To see how growth responds to one driver (say radiation), we cannot simply vary it in the equation while holding the others at their mean, because in real weather the drivers move together. Here thermal time and day length have correlation 0.97:

Z <- observed_points(drv, tr)                   # the weather that actually occurred (rows = year x day)
round(cor(Z), 2)

       TT    DL   RAW   RAD
TT   1.00  0.97 -0.65  0.72
DL   0.97  1.00 -0.67  0.74
RAW -0.65 -0.67  1.00 -0.58
RAD  0.72  0.74 -0.58  1.00


Accumulated local effects (ALE) avoid asking the model about weather that never happens: within each small interval of the driver they compare the model with the driver at the two ends of the interval, using the real values of the other drivers, then add up the changes.
ale_curve <- function(rate, Z, j, K = 24) {
  e <- unique(quantile(Z[, j], seq(0, 1, length.out = K + 1))); nb_ <- length(e) - 1
  b <- pmin(pmax(findInterval(Z[, j], e), 1), nb_)
  Zu <- Z; Zl <- Z; Zu[, j] <- e[b + 1]; Zl[, j] <- e[b]
  d <- rate(Zu) - rate(Zl); nb <- tabulate(b, nb_)
  md <- vapply(split(d, factor(b, levels = seq_len(nb_))), sum, 0) / pmax(nb, 1)
  A <- c(0, cumsum(md)); mid <- (A[-1] + A[-length(A)]) / 2
  data.frame(z = e, effect = A - sum(mid * nb) / sum(nb))
}
For contrast, the classical partial dependence (PDP) sets the driver to a value for all observations at once:

pdp <- function(rate, Z, j, grid) sapply(grid, function(v) { Zv <- Z; Zv[, j] <- v; mean(rate(Zv)) })

curves <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(drv$drivers), function(j) {
  a <- ale_curve(rate, Z, j); p <- pdp(rate, Z, j, a$z)
  x <- a$z * drv$scale[j] + drv$center[j]                                     # back to natural units
  rbind(data.frame(driver = drv$drivers[j], x = x, effect = a$effect, method = "ALE"),
        data.frame(driver = drv$drivers[j], x = x, effect = p - mean(p) + 0, method = "PDP"))
}))
curves$driver <- factor(curves$driver, c("TT", "DL", "RAW", "RAD"))


ggplot(curves, aes(x, effect, colour = method, linetype = method)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~driver, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(dgxe[c("blue", "orange")])) +
  labs(x = "driver value (TT: degree-days, DL: hours, RAW: 0 to 1, RAD: MJ/m2/day)", y = "effect on growth rate (t/ha/day)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) + theme_dgxe()








For this library the two curves lie on top of each other. That is expected: the library is a sum of one-driver polynomials, so the effect of one driver does not depend on the others. The methods only differ once the model contains interactions. Refit with the 37-term library, which adds products of drivers:

Theta2 <- make_library(drv, pairs = TRUE); gram2 <- gram_stats(Theta2, tr)
f2 <- fit_years(gram2, seq_along(tr$years), fit_ssr, k = 20)
rate2 <- function(Z) as.vector(library_matrix(Z, pairs = TRUE) %*% f2$mu)
curves2 <- do.call(rbind, lapply(1:2, function(j) {
  a <- ale_curve(rate2, Z, j); p <- pdp(rate2, Z, j, a$z); x <- a$z * drv$scale[j] + drv$center[j]
  rbind(data.frame(driver = drv$drivers[j], x = x, effect = a$effect, method = "ALE"),
        data.frame(driver = drv$drivers[j], x = x, effect = p - mean(p), method = "PDP")) }))


ggplot(curves2, aes(x, effect, colour = method, linetype = method)) + geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) + facet_wrap(~driver, scales = "free_x") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(dgxe[c("blue", "orange")])) +
  labs(x = "driver value", y = "effect on growth rate (t/ha/day)", colour = NULL, linetype = NULL) + theme_dgxe()








Where the curves now differ, partial dependence is averaging over weather combinations that do not occur (for example a cold season with very long days), so the ALE curve is the one to interpret.






NoteIdea



A fitted equation is a model you can interrogate. The coefficients are a way to store the equation; the curves are how you read it. Each curve answers one question: “if this driver were a bit higher on a day like those in the data, how would growth change?”








ImportantPitfall



Thermal time is a clock, not a temperature. Its curve shows how growth changes as the season advances (as degree-days accumulate), not how the crop responds to a hot day. Do not read the TT curve as a temperature response. Because TT and DL are 0.97 correlated, the model cannot separate them well; read their curves together.








TipCheck



Do the curves look agronomically plausible? Water (RAW) should not reduce growth as it rises, and radiation should not reduce growth as it increases. A curve that goes the wrong way is a prompt to look at the data, not to publish.








CautionSwap



Replace mu with the coefficients of any other fit (fit_years(gram, years, fit_ridge), or the 37-term library) and re-run the plotting code unchanged; rate() is the only place the model enters.

title: 4 · Fitting
text: You needgram (A and b per genotype and year) from step 3.You getcoefficients from OLS, ridge, sparse (SSR) and lasso fits, and a feel for which terms matter.

title: 4 · Fitting
text:
One pooled problem
To start simply, pool all genotypes and all years into one regression. We add up the per-trajectory statistics and put every library column on a common scale (unit root-mean-square), so coefficient sizes are comparable.

st <- sum_years(gram, seq_along(tr$years))        # add up all years, keep genotypes apart
A  <- apply(st$A, c(2, 3), sum)                   # add up genotypes too
b  <- colSums(st$b)
sc <- scale_gram(A, b, n = sum(st$n))             # scaled normal equations
terms <- gram$names

title: 4 · Fitting
section: A fitting method is a function fit(A, b, ...)
text:
A fitting method is a function fit(A, b, ...)
Every method takes the same two objects and returns list(coef, support).
fit_ols <- function(A, b, ...) {
  list(coef = solve(A, b), support = seq_along(b))
}
fit_ridge <- function(A, b, lambda = 0.01, ...) {
  list(coef = solve(A + lambda * mean(diag(A)) * diag(nrow(A)), b), support = seq_along(b))
}
fit_ssr <- function(A, b, k = 8, alpha = 1e-6, ...) {
  S <- seq_along(b)
  repeat {
    co <- solve(A[S, S, drop = FALSE] + alpha * diag(length(S)), b[S])
    if (length(S) <= k) break
    S <- S[-which.min(abs(co))]
  }
  coef <- numeric(length(b)); coef[S] <- co
  list(coef = coef, support = S)
}
Ordinary least squares uses every term. Ridge shrinks them. Sequential thresholding (SSR) refits, removes the smallest coefficient, and repeats until \(k\) terms remain.

ols <- fit_ols(sc$A, sc$b)
rdg <- fit_ridge(sc$A, sc$b, lambda = 0.01)
ssr <- fit_ssr(sc$A, sc$b, k = 8)
tab <- data.frame(term = terms, OLS = ols$coef, ridge = rdg$coef, SSR_8 = ssr$coef)
tab[, -1] <- round(tab[, -1], 3); tab

title: 4 · Fitting
text:
Watching the sparse fit decide
SSR removes terms one at a time. The order shows what the data cannot do without:

S <- seq_along(terms); out <- character(0)
while (length(S) > 1) {
  co <- solve(sc$A[S, S, drop = FALSE] + 1e-6 * diag(length(S)), sc$b[S])
  w <- which.min(abs(co)); out <- c(out, terms[S[w]]); S <- S[-w]
}
data.frame(removed_in_order = out, terms_left_after = 12:1)

   removed_in_order terms_left_after
1             RAW^3               12
2             RAD^3               11
3             RAD^2               10
4               RAD                9
5               RAW                8
6                DL                7
7              TT^3                6
8                TT                5
9             RAW^2                4
10             DL^3                3
11             DL^2                2
12             TT^2                1

c(last_standing = terms[S])

last_standing 
          "1" 


The first terms to go are the high powers of radiation and water, and what survives longest are the constant and the powers of thermal time and day length. Be careful with this ranking: it is not an importance measure. A term can be dropped because its effect is shared with correlated powers of the same driver, and the order depends on the library. The honest question is how many terms the model needs to predict well on unseen years, which is the topic of step 5; step 6 then reads the fitted curves rather than individual coefficients.

title: 4 · Fitting
section: Writing your own method: lasso in ten lines
text:
Writing your own method: lasso in ten lines
Nothing above is special. Any method that turns (A, b) into coefficients works. As an example, the lasso written as coordinate descent on the same scaled normal equations:

fit_lasso <- function(A, b, lambda = 0.01, iters = 2000, ...) {
  xi <- numeric(length(b))
  for (it in seq_len(iters)) {
    old <- xi
    for (j in seq_along(b)) {
      r <- b[j] - sum(A[j, -j] * xi[-j])                         # partial residual
      xi[j] <- sign(r) * max(abs(r) - lambda, 0) / A[j, j]       # soft threshold
    }
    if (max(abs(xi - old)) < 1e-9) break
  }
  list(coef = xi, support = which(xi != 0))
}
las <- fit_lasso(sc$A, sc$b, lambda = 2e-4)
setNames(round(las$coef, 3), terms)

     1     TT   TT^2   TT^3     DL   DL^2   DL^3    RAW  RAW^2  RAW^3    RAD 
 0.149  0.000 -0.034  0.004 -0.003 -0.045  0.023  0.010 -0.017  0.000  0.005 
 RAD^2  RAD^3 
-0.003  0.000 








NoteIdea



The method is a plug-in. Steps 2 and 3 produced A and b; step 4 turns them into coefficients; steps 5 to 8 only need coef and support. Replace the fitting function and nothing else changes.








TipCheck



OLS and ridge should be close (the problem is well conditioned). Sparse fits should agree with OLS on the terms they keep. If a sparse fit changes sign on a large coefficient, the library has collinear terms.








CautionSwap



Try fit_ssr(sc$A, sc$b, k = 5), fit_ridge(..., lambda = 1), or fit_lasso(..., lambda = 1e-3). The next step shows how to judge them honestly: on years the model has never seen.

title: 2 · The data
text:
What the data are
The data come from APSIM wheat simulations at Narrabri, a site in northern New South Wales: 199 genotypes grown in 31 years (1983 to 2013). Every genotype-year has daily biomass from 15 days after sowing until that genotype’s own maturity. Because weather is the same for all genotypes in a given year, we keep weather and biomass in separate tables.

title: Dynamic GxE from scratch
text: A crop does not jump to its final yield; it grows a little every day, and how much it grows depends on that day’s weather and on the genotype. This workshop shows how to learn that daily growth rule from data, using nothing but base R and a few lines per step.

title: Dynamic GxE from scratch
text:
The question we follow

Can we learn the daily growth rule of wheat from simulated field trials, and use it to predict a year the model has never seen?

We work with one site (Narrabri), 199 wheat genotypes and 31 years of daily data from the public APSIM wheat simulations. The method is SINDy (sparse identification of nonlinear dynamics): write the growth rate as a combination of a few candidate functions of the weather, and let the data decide which ones matter.

title: Dynamic GxE from scratch
text:
The pipeline
Every step is a small function with a clear input and output. Any step can be replaced without touching the others, for example a different fitting method or a different library of candidate functions.



1 · The idea


A model of change is a running total of daily growth. A toy example, solved with lm.




2 · The data


Two plain tables: daily weather and daily biomass.




3 · Library and design matrix


Candidate functions of the weather, stacked into a regression problem.




4 · Fitting


OLS, ridge and sparse regression, all behind one signature.




5 · Simulate and validate


Roll the equation forward and test it on held-out years.




6 · Reading the model


Response curves: what the equation says about weather and growth.




7 · Genotypes


A shared model plus genotype deviations, and ranking lines.




8 · When it breaks


Wrong libraries, collinear drivers, one-step versus rollout fit.




9 · Going further


Adding crop knowledge, coupled states, and the Bayesian version.

title: Dynamic GxE from scratch
text:
How to follow along
Every page runs on its own and takes seconds. The whole pipeline, including leave-one-year-out cross-validation over all 199 genotypes, runs in about ten seconds.
# base R is enough; ggplot2 is only used for the plots
install.packages("ggplot2")
source("R/functions.R")      # all modelling functions, plain base R
Start at Set up, or jump straight to the idea.






NoteWhere the data come from



The data are simulated biomass and daily weather for four Australian sites, from Bustos-Korts et al. (2019), From QTLs to adaptation landscapes: using genotype-to-phenotype models to characterize G×E over time, Frontiers in Plant Science 10:1540. Because the data are simulated, the true crop parameters are known, which lets us check what the method recovers.

title: 1 · The idea
text: You neednothing yet: this page uses a toy example, not the real data.You getthe core trick of the whole workshop: learning a rate equation is a regression.

title: 1 · The idea
section: A crop as a running total
text:
A crop as a running total
Think of the biomass of a crop as a bank balance. Every day some growth is added, and how much is added depends on today’s balance (a bigger plant intercepts more light) and on today’s weather. Written as a rule for the daily change:
\[
y_{t+1} = y_t + \underbrace{f(y_t, u_t)}_{\text{growth today}}
\]
This is a difference equation, and its continuous cousin is the ordinary differential equation (ODE) \(\mathrm{d}y/\mathrm{d}t = f(y, u)\). Crop models such as APSIM do exactly this, day by day. The whole question of the workshop is: what is \(f\)?

title: 1 · The idea
text:
A toy crop
Let growth be logistic (fast when small, slowing near a ceiling \(K\)) and let a stress period in the weather reduce it:
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} = r\,y\left(1 - \frac{y}{K}\right) S(t), \qquad S(t) = 1 - \alpha\,(1 - e(t))
\]
Here \(e(t)\) is a weather signal that dips during a stress event, and \(\alpha\) is the sensitivity to it. We simulate one season with a daily step:

r <- 0.12; K <- 5; alpha <- 0.8          # growth rate, ceiling, stress sensitivity
n <- 100; day <- 0:n
e <- 1 - 0.9 * exp(-((day - 40) / 12)^2)  # weather signal: stress around day 40
S <- 1 - alpha * (1 - e)                  # growth modulator

y <- numeric(n + 1); y[1] <- 0.05
for (t in 1:n) y[t + 1] <- y[t] + r * y[t] * (1 - y[t] / K) * S[t]










The crop slows down when the stress hits and recovers afterwards, so the curve has a shoulder.

title: 1 · The idea
section: The trick: a rate equation is a regression
text:
The trick: a rate equation is a regression
Suppose we did not know \(f\). We would observe \(y\) and \(e\) every day, and we would compute the daily increments \(z_t = y_{t+1} - y_t\). If we guess that \(f\) is a combination of simple candidate functions (a library),
\[
z_t \approx \sum_{j} \xi_j\, \theta_j(y_t, e_t),
\]
then the unknown coefficients \(\xi_j\) enter linearly. This is an ordinary linear regression. Our library is every product of \(y\) and \(e\) up to second power:

library_toy <- function(y, e) cbind(y = y, `y^2` = y^2, e = e, `e^2` = e^2,
                                    `y*e` = y * e, `y^2*e` = y^2 * e, `y*e^2` = y * e^2, `y^2*e^2` = y^2 * e^2)

X <- library_toy(y[-(n + 1)], e[-(n + 1)])   # library on days 0 .. n-1
z <- diff(y)                                 # daily increments
fit <- lm(z ~ X - 1)                         # no intercept: no constant in the library

Expanding the true equation gives the exact coefficients we should find: only \(y\), \(y^2\), \(y\,e\) and \(y^2 e\) appear, and the four terms that do not belong are zero.

truth <- c(r * (1 - alpha), -r * (1 - alpha) / K, 0, 0, r * alpha, -r * alpha / K, 0, 0)
fitted <- setNames(coef(fit), colnames(X))
round(rbind(truth = truth, fitted = fitted), 5)

           y     y^2 e e^2   y*e   y^2*e y*e^2 y^2*e^2
truth  0.024 -0.0048 0   0 0.096 -0.0192     0       0
fitted 0.024 -0.0048 0   0 0.096 -0.0192     0       0








NoteIdea



The regression found the equation exactly: four true terms recovered, four zero terms recovered as zero. Learning an ODE from data is just a linear regression of daily increments on a library of candidate functions. Everything else in this workshop (sparsity, genotypes, validation) builds on this one step.

title: 1 · The idea
text:
Make it break: add noise
Real measurements are noisy. A small error in \(y\) becomes a large error in the increment \(z_t = y_{t+1} - y_t\) (a difference of two noisy numbers), and the library terms are strongly correlated, so ordinary least squares struggles.

set.seed(1)
yn <- y + rnorm(n + 1, sd = 0.01)          # 0.01 t/ha of measurement noise
Xn <- library_toy(yn[-(n + 1)], e[-(n + 1)]); zn <- diff(yn)
ols <- setNames(coef(lm(zn ~ Xn - 1)), colnames(Xn))

A sparse fit keeps only the few terms that matter. Here is the simplest version, which repeatedly refits and removes the smallest coefficient until four terms are left (fit_ssr is defined in step 4):

A <- crossprod(Xn) / n                     # the regression, as normal equations
b <- as.numeric(crossprod(Xn, zn)) / n
sparse <- setNames(fit_ssr(A, b, k = 4)$coef, colnames(Xn))


round(rbind(truth = truth, `ols (noisy)` = ols, `sparse, 4 terms` = sparse), 3)

                    y    y^2      e   e^2   y*e  y^2*e  y*e^2 y^2*e^2
truth           0.024 -0.005  0.000 0.000 0.096 -0.019  0.000   0.000
ols (noisy)     0.030 -0.009 -0.024 0.024 0.116 -0.020 -0.025   0.004
sparse, 4 terms 0.017  0.000  0.001 0.000 0.101 -0.024  0.000   0.000


OLS spreads weight over all eight terms, including some that are truly zero. The sparse fit keeps three of the four true terms (\(y\), \(y\,e\), \(y^2 e\)) and swaps the fourth (\(y^2\)) for a term that does not belong (\(e\), with a tiny coefficient). It is much closer to the truth than OLS, but not perfect. With three times more noise (sd = 0.03) even the sparse fit loses the structure: a model needs enough signal.






ImportantPitfall



Noise in the state is amplified by differencing. With only 8–13 observations per season (typical for field trials) you should integrate the equation over each interval instead of differencing, which is what the research code does for field data. Here the data are simulated daily, so differencing is fine.








CautionSwap



Try changing sd = 0.01 to 0.005 or 0.02, or the number of terms k to 3 or 6. How many terms survive? At what noise level does the structure disappear?

title: 1 · The idea
text:
What comes next
In the real problem the “state” is biomass, the “weather” is four measured drivers (thermal time, day length, water availability and radiation), and there are 199 genotypes. The next page looks at those data.

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
text:
From weather to drivers
Each driver is standardised (mean 0, standard deviation 1) so that coefficients are comparable and a cubic in a driver stays well behaved. We only use weather here, never biomass, so this step cannot leak anything about the response.
make_drivers <- function (wx, drivers = c("TT", "DL", "RAW", "RAD")) 
{
    years <- sort(unique(wx$year))
    das0 <- min(wx$das)
    nd <- max(wx$das) - das0 + 1
    U <- array(NA, c(length(years), nd, length(drivers)), dimnames = list(years, 
        NULL, drivers))
    for (i in seq_along(years)) {
        w <- wx[wx$year == years[i], ]
        U[i, w$das - das0 + 1, ] <- as.matrix(w[, drivers])
        last <- max(w$das) - das0 + 1
        if (last < nd) 
            U[i, (last + 1):nd, ] <- matrix(rep(U[i, last, ], 
                each = nd - last), nd - last)
    }
    center <- apply(U, 3, mean)
    scale <- apply(U, 3, function(x) sqrt(mean((x - mean(x))^2)))
    for (j in seq_along(drivers)) U[, , j] <- (U[, , j] - center[j])/scale[j]
    list(U = U, years = years, das0 = das0, drivers = drivers, 
        center = center, scale = scale)
}

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
text:
The library of candidate functions
The growth rate on day \(t\) is modelled as a combination of candidate functions of that day’s drivers \(u_t = (\text{TT}, \text{DL}, \text{RAW}, \text{RAD})\):
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}y}{\mathrm{d}t} \approx \sum_{j=1}^{K} \xi_j\,\theta_j(u_t), \qquad \theta_j \in \{\,1,\ \text{TT},\ \text{TT}^2,\ \text{TT}^3,\ \text{DL},\ \dots,\ \text{RAD}^3\,\}
\]
That is a constant and a cubic polynomial in each driver: \(K = 1 + 3 \times 4 = 13\) terms.
library_matrix <- function (Z, degree = 3, pairs = FALSE) 
{
    pw <- function(x, p) if (p == 1) 
        x
    else paste0(x, "^", p)
    d <- colnames(Z)
    cols <- list(rep(1, nrow(Z)))
    nm <- "1"
    for (j in seq_along(d)) for (p in seq_len(degree)) {
        cols[[length(cols) + 1]] <- Z[, j]^p
        nm <- c(nm, pw(d[j], p))
    }
    if (pairs) 
        for (i in 1:(length(d) - 1)) for (j in (i + 1):length(d)) for (p in 1:2) for (q in 1:2) {
            cols[[length(cols) + 1]] <- Z[, i]^p * Z[, j]^q
            nm <- c(nm, paste0(pw(d[i], p), "*", pw(d[j], q)))
        }
    L <- do.call(cbind, cols)
    colnames(L) <- nm
    L
}
make_library <- function (drv, degree = 3, pairs = FALSE) 
{
    nd <- dim(drv$U)
    Z <- matrix(drv$U, ncol = nd[3])
    colnames(Z) <- drv$drivers
    L <- library_matrix(Z, degree, pairs)
    array(L, c(nd[1:2], ncol(L)), dimnames = list(NULL, NULL, 
        colnames(L)))
}

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
text:
The response: daily growth increments
For every genotype-year we need the biomass trajectory as an array Y[genotype, year, day], with NA after maturity.
make_trajectories <- function (traj, drv, var = "biomass") 
{
    gen <- sort(unique(traj$genotype))
    nd <- dim(drv$U)[2]
    Y <- array(NA, c(length(gen), length(drv$years), nd), dimnames = list(gen, 
        drv$years, NULL))
    Y[cbind(match(traj$genotype, gen), match(traj$year, drv$years), 
        traj$das - drv$das0 + 1)] <- traj[[var]]
    nend <- apply(Y, c(1, 2), function(v) sum(!is.na(v)) - 1)
    list(Y = Y, nend = nend, genotypes = gen, years = drv$years, 
        das0 = drv$das0)
}

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
text:
The design matrix
Stacking every step of every trajectory gives an ordinary regression problem \(z \approx X\xi\). Here it is for three genotypes:
build_design <- function (Theta, tr, genotypes = tr$genotypes) 
{
    X <- list()
    z <- list()
    id <- list()
    for (g in genotypes) for (y in seq_along(tr$years)) {
        gi <- match(g, tr$genotypes)
        n <- tr$nend[gi, y]
        v <- tr$Y[gi, y, 1:(n + 1)]
        X[[length(X) + 1]] <- matrix(Theta[y, 1:n, ], n)
        z[[length(z) + 1]] <- diff(v)
        id[[length(id) + 1]] <- data.frame(genotype = g, year = tr$years[y], 
            day = 0:(n - 1))
    }
    X <- do.call(rbind, X)
    colnames(X) <- dimnames(Theta)[[3]]
    list(X = X, z = unlist(z), id = do.call(rbind, id))
}

title: 3 · Library and design matrix
section: The normal equations: everything a fit needs
text:
The normal equations: everything a fit needs
For any linear method, the data enter only through \(A = X^\top X\) and \(b = X^\top z\). We compute them per genotype and per year, so that cross-validation later only needs to add and subtract small matrices (for 199 genotypes the full design matrix has 850,000 rows).
gram_stats <- function (Theta, tr) 
{
    G <- dim(tr$Y)[1]
    ny <- length(tr$years)
    K <- dim(Theta)[3]
    A <- array(0, c(G, ny, K, K))
    b <- array(0, c(G, ny, K))
    for (g in seq_len(G)) for (y in seq_len(ny)) {
        n <- tr$nend[g, y]
        X <- matrix(Theta[y, 1:n, ], n)
        A[g, y, , ] <- crossprod(X)
        b[g, y, ] <- crossprod(X, diff(tr$Y[g, y, 1:(n + 1)]))
    }
    list(A = A, b = b, n = tr$nend, names = dimnames(Theta)[[3]])
}

gram <- gram_stats(Theta, tr)
A <- apply(gram$A[1:3, , , ], c(3, 4), sum); b <- apply(gram$b[1:3, , ], 3, sum)
c(max_diff_A = max(abs(A - crossprod(des$X))), max_diff_b = max(abs(b - crossprod(des$X, des$z))))

  max_diff_A   max_diff_b 
4.569301e-09 2.160050e-12 

max(abs(solve(A, b) - coef(lm(des$z ~ des$X - 1))))        # same coefficients as lm

NoteIdea



The library and the data are separate. Once A and b exist, a fitting method never sees weather or biomass again, only these two small objects. That is why any regression method (OLS, ridge, sparse, lasso) can be swapped in at the next step.








TipCheck



A and b built from the per-trajectory pieces equal crossprod(X) and crossprod(X, z) from the explicit design matrix up to rounding, and solve(A, b) equals lm.

title: 5 · Roll forward and validate
text: You needTheta, tr, gram and a fitting method from step 4.You getpredicted biomass trajectories for held-out years, and a table comparing methods.

title: 5 · Roll forward and validate
section: Solving the equation is a running total
text:
Solving the equation is a running total
The fitted rule says how fast biomass grows on each day, given that day’s weather. Because the library depends only on the weather, there is nothing to integrate numerically: biomass is the starting value plus the running sum of daily growth.
\[
y(t) = y_0 + \sum_{s<t} \Theta(u_s)\,\xi
\]
simulate <- function(xi, Theta_y, y0) {
  inc <- Theta_y[-nrow(Theta_y), , drop = FALSE] %*% t(xi)         # (days-1) x genotype increments
  sweep(rbind(0, apply(inc, 2, cumsum)), 2, y0, "+")               # day x genotype
}

title: 5 · Roll forward and validate
text:
One held-out year
Fit on all years except 1998, then predict 1998 from its weather alone. fit_years chooses the shared terms with the chosen method, then adds a small shrunk deviation for each genotype (step 7).

yv    <- match(1998, tr$years)
train <- setdiff(seq_along(tr$years), yv)
f     <- fit_years(gram, train, fit_ssr, k = 12)
y0    <- apply(tr$Y[, train, 1], 1, mean)                       # starting biomass: training mean
pred  <- simulate(f$xi, Theta[yv, , ], y0)                      # day x genotype
f$names[f$support]                                              # the 12 shared terms

    APSIM = tr$Y[g, yv, 1:n], SINDy = pred[1:n, g]) }

title: 5 · Roll forward and validate
text:
Leave-one-year-out cross-validation
Repeat for every year: each year is predicted by a model that never saw it. Seeing only weather forecasts, not APSIM biomass, is the point; this is the honest test.
cv_blocked <- function(Theta, tr, gram, fitter = fit_ssr, k = 12, lam_mu = 1e-4, lam_g = 0.01, ...) {
  ny <- length(tr$years); G <- length(tr$genotypes); nd <- dim(Theta)[2]
  P <- array(NA_real_, c(G, ny, nd)); S_all <- vector("list", ny)
  for (yv in seq_len(ny)) {
    train <- setdiff(seq_len(ny), yv); f <- fit_years(gram, train, fitter, k, lam_mu, lam_g, ...)
    y0 <- apply(tr$Y[, train, 1, drop = FALSE], 1, mean)                        # initial biomass: mean of training years
    P[, yv, ] <- t(simulate(f$xi, Theta[yv, , ], y0)); S_all[[yv]] <- f$support
  }
  list(pred = P, support = S_all)
}
evaluate <- function(P, tr, fixed_day = 99) {
  G <- dim(P)[1]; ny <- dim(P)[2]; se <- 0; cnt <- 0; fin <- numeric(0)
  for (g in seq_len(G)) for (y in seq_len(ny)) {
    n <- tr$nend[g, y]; d <- 2:(n + 1)                      # day index 1..n (day 0 is the given start)
    se <- se + sum((P[g, y, d] - tr$Y[g, y, d])^2); cnt <- cnt + length(d)
    fin <- c(fin, P[g, y, n + 1] - tr$Y[g, y, n + 1])
  }
  c(trajectory_rmse = sqrt(se / cnt), fixed_day_rmse = sqrt(mean((P[, , fixed_day] - tr$Y[, , fixed_day])^2, na.rm = TRUE)),
    maturity_rmse = sqrt(mean(fin^2)))
}

A baseline that uses no weather
How much does the weather add? A simple competitor: predict each genotype’s biomass curve by the average of its own curves in the other years.

base <- array(NA_real_, dim(tr$Y))
for (y in seq_along(tr$years)) base[, y, ] <- apply(tr$Y[, -y, , drop = FALSE], c(1, 3), mean, na.rm = TRUE)
for (g in 1:dim(base)[1]) for (y in 1:dim(base)[2]) {
  v <- base[g, y, ]; ok <- which(!is.nan(v)); v[is.nan(v)] <- v[max(ok)]               # after the last other year ends: hold the last mean
  base[g, y, ] <- v; base[g, y, 1] <- tr$Y[g, y, 1]                                    # same start as the model
}

Swap the fitting method
Because every method has the signature fit(A, b, ...), comparing them is one loop:

  m <- methods[[nm]]; cv <- do.call(cv_blocked, c(list(Theta, tr, gram, m[[1]]), m[-1]))
  data.frame(method = nm, t(round(evaluate(cv$pred, tr), 3))) })))

section: How many terms? A larger library
text:
How many terms? A larger library
With the 13-term library, sparsity buys little: it is already small. Add products of drivers (pairs = TRUE, 37 terms) and the picture changes:

Theta2 <- make_library(drv, pairs = TRUE); gram2 <- gram_stats(Theta2, tr)
ks <- c(6, 8, 12, 16, 20, 30, 37)
rk <- cached("rmse_vs_k_pairs.rds", data.frame(k = ks, rmse = sapply(ks, function(k) evaluate(cv_blocked(Theta2, tr, gram2, fit_ssr, k = k)$pred, tr)[1])))


ggplot(rk, aes(k, rmse)) + geom_line(colour = dgxe[["blue"]], linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(colour = dgxe[["blue"]], size = 2.4) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = res$trajectory_rmse[res$method == "OLS"], colour = dgxe[["orange"]], linetype = 2) +
  annotate("text", x = 37, y = res$trajectory_rmse[res$method == "OLS"], label = "13-term OLS", vjust = -0.6, hjust = 1, colour = dgxe[["orange"]], size = 3.4) +
  labs(x = "number of terms kept (SSR)", y = "held-out trajectory RMSE (t/ha)") + theme_dgxe()














NoteIdea



Predicting forward is a running total, and it is judged on years the model never saw. Error accumulates along the rollout, so this is a stricter test than one-step prediction. A model can fit daily increments well and still drift.








TipCheck



The model should beat the weather-free lookup, and the held-out error should be larger than the in-sample error. Plot a few trajectories: errors that grow steadily through the season point to a missing driver.








ImportantPitfall



Never validate by randomly holding out days. Neighbouring days of one year are nearly identical, and a year is the unit of independent weather, so we hold out whole years. The same goes for genotypes of the same year when you ask about new weather.

title: 7 · Genotypes
text:
Shared plus deviation
All 199 genotypes grow in a similar way, and each differs a little. We write the coefficient vector of genotype \(g\) as
\[
\xi_g = \mu + \delta_g,
\]
where \(\mu\) is shared (found in step 4 from the pooled data) and \(\delta_g\) is a small, ridge-shrunk correction estimated from that genotype’s own 31 seasons. The support (which terms are active) is shared, so every genotype has the same equation form and only the numbers differ.
fit_hier <- function(Ag, bg, support, lam_mu = 1e-4, lam_g = 0.01) {
  K <- dim(Ag)[2]; k <- length(support); G <- dim(Ag)[1]
  Apool <- apply(Ag[, support, support, drop = FALSE], c(2, 3), sum); bpool <- colSums(bg[, support, drop = FALSE])
  mu <- numeric(K); mu[support] <- solve(Apool + lam_mu * mean(diag(Apool)) * diag(k), bpool)
  delta <- matrix(0, G, K)
  for (g in seq_len(G)) {
    Aq <- Ag[g, support, support]; tr <- sum(diag(Aq)) / k
    delta[g, support] <- solve(Aq + lam_g * tr * diag(k), bg[g, support] - Aq %*% mu[support])
  }
  list(mu = mu, delta = delta, xi = sweep(delta, 2, mu, "+"), support = support)
}

title: 7 · Genotypes
section: Does it rank genotypes better than a lookup?
text:
Does it rank genotypes better than a lookup?
Breeders often care more about the ranking of genotypes in a given year than about absolute biomass. For every year, we compare the predicted and APSIM ranking of the 199 genotypes at a fixed day using the Spearman correlation, and by the overlap of the predicted and true top 10%. The competitor is again the no-weather lookup (the genotype’s mean in the other years).
rank_scores <- function(Pd, Yd, top = 0.1) {
  k <- max(1, round(top * nrow(Yd)))
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(ncol(Yd)), function(y) data.frame(
    year = y, rho = cor(Pd[, y], Yd[, y], method = "spearman"),
    top = length(intersect(order(-Pd[, y])[1:k], order(-Yd[, y])[1:k])) / k)))
}
lookup_baseline <- function(Yd) (rowSums(Yd) - Yd) / (ncol(Yd) - 1)

cv   <- cv_blocked(Theta, tr, gram, fit_ssr, k = 12)
days <- c(35, 50, 63, 84, 99)                         # day index; das = day index + 14
out  <- do.call(rbind, lapply(days, function(d) {
  Yd <- tr$Y[, , d]; a <- rank_scores(cv$pred[, , d], Yd); b <- rank_scores(lookup_baseline(Yd), Yd)
  data.frame(das = d + tr$das0 - 1, method = c("SINDy", "lookup"),
             rho = c(mean(a$rho), mean(b$rho)), top10 = c(mean(a$top), mean(b$top))) }))
out$rho <- round(out$rho, 3); out$top10 <- round(out$top10, 3); out

  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(dgxe[c("orange", "blue")])) + labs(x = "days after sowing", y = NULL, colour = NULL) + theme_dgxe()








Early in the season the lookup wins: the ranking has not yet been shaped by the weather, so each genotype’s average curve already orders them well. Later, when the season’s weather has started to reorder genotypes, the model that uses the weather overtakes the lookup. This is what we would hope for from a model that responds to weather, but it is also an honest reminder that the lookup is hard to beat when there is nothing to learn from the weather.






NoteIdea



Sharing strength across genotypes. One genotype has only 31 trajectories, which would not support a 12-term model on its own. Pooling fixes the form of the equation; shrinkage lets each genotype adjust the numbers only as far as its own data justify.








TipCheck



Plot the deviations \(\delta_g\) for one term across genotypes: they should be small compared to \(\mu\) and roughly centred on zero. If they are large, the shared structure is not capturing what genotypes have in common.








ImportantPitfall



These ranking results are for genotypes seen in training and predicted in held-out years. Predicting a brand-new genotype needs extra information (such as its parameters) and is not tested here.

title: 9 · Going further
section: The weather-only model has a limitation
text:
The weather-only model has a limitation
In steps 4 to 8 growth depends on the weather and on the day, but not on the crop’s own state. That is why solving the equation is just a running total. Real crops are different: more leaf area means more light intercepted, which means faster biomass growth. A model that captures this is a coupled system with two states,
\[
\frac{\mathrm{d}L}{\mathrm{d}t} = f_L(L, B, u_t), \qquad \frac{\mathrm{d}B}{\mathrm{d}t} = f_B(L, B, u_t),
\]
with \(L\) the leaf area index and \(B\) the biomass. Now the state appears on the right-hand side, so solving needs a proper ODE solver and cannot be done with cumsum. The normal-equation machinery of steps 3 to 5 still applies for fitting (the regression is still linear in the coefficients), but the rollout is a numerical integration, and errors can feed back on themselves.

title: 9 · Going further
section: Use physical knowledge in the library
text:
Use physical knowledge in the library
A useful library term for biomass is the light intercepted by the canopy, \(I = 1 - \exp(-0.5\,L)\). This is plant physiology put into the dictionary as one candidate term: \(\mathrm{d}B/\mathrm{d}t \ni I \cdot \text{RAD}\).

title: 9 · Going further
text:
Other directions

Other regression methods. Anything with the fit(A, b, ...) signature works. Bayesian versions of the regression, with sparsity-inducing priors, give uncertainty for the coefficients but are slower and need extra packages.
Other sites. We used one site. Pooling sites adds site-level variation in the weather and is a natural next step.
New genotypes. Predicting an unseen genotype needs information about it, such as its parameter values, and has not been shown here.
Other responses. The same pipeline applies to other state variables; step 8 showed one example (LAI).







NoteIdea



The workflow of this workshop, a library of candidate terms, a regression, a rollout, and a validation on unseen years, does not change when the model becomes coupled. What changes is the rollout (a solver) and how carefully the library has to be built.
